body_en:
Start with one number. In 2016, China's baijiu output peaked at 13.584 million kiloliters. By 2025 it was down to 3.549 million — a collapse of 74%.

Hence the question everyone asks: why can't Chinese people drink anymore?

My answer runs the other way. It is not that Chinese people can't drink. It is that they have finally started living like human beings. The day China realizes that drinking anything over 20% ABV is a pure 24-karat act of self-harm, everyone's life gets better.

Twenty Percent Is Fermentation's Ceiling

Begin with a basic fact: no fermented drink above 20% exists in nature.

Yeast turns sugar into alcohol, and once the alcohol reaches the mid-teens, it kills the yeast itself. Fermentation stops. That is a hard biological limit, not a matter of craft.

So where do port and sherry, sitting around 20%, come from? Someone pours in outside alcohol, kills the yeast early, and leaves sugar behind to mask a mediocre wine — a fortified drink designed to be served after dinner. Fundamentally, it is a poor man's pleasure. Port is called Britain's national wine, and Cameron once served it to a visiting Chinese leader; the British treat it as a treasure. At home, though, it is a degraded knockoff of proper sherry — a fortified fake whose only job is to add a few degrees so drinkers feel they got their money's worth.

The shaoguo liquor along the Grand Canal in the mid-to-late Qing dynasty ran on the same logic: coarsely distilled grain spirit, made to revive exhausted canal workers. It was never culture. It was cheap, and it hit hard.

Distilled Spirits Were a Logistics Hack

Baijiu, shaojiu, every distilled spirit — the reason they exist is not romantic at all. Freight.

Before container ships, before railways and trucks, the cheapest way to move alcohol was to concentrate it, ship it, and dilute it at the destination. It is exactly the logic of frozen orange juice concentrate — and nobody drinks concentrate straight from the can, because it burns. Spirits are alcohol in concentrate form. Their original job was to be a cocktail base: you saved the freight, then you rehydrated the product yourself.

No people on earth abuse themselves quite like the Slavs, throwing high-proof alcohol straight down their throats. Any spirit that cannot be rehydrated — cannot be cut with water into something pleasant and low-proof — is a product of backward technology and an unenlightened age. It just happens to have a large, loyal customer base, so over time it acquired a costume of culture: mass delusion, a loyalty test, a cheap anesthetic.

Things that are naturally obsolete take only a generation or two to lose their magic. Once every convenience store sells disposable lighters, who still strikes a flint? Pagers and Walkmans — plenty of young people today cannot even tell you what they were for.

Next to the mini bottles of spirits in a convenience store, there is a printed guide showing you exactly which soda and which cup of ice turns them into a cocktail. That is the correct way to open a bottle of spirits.

Baijiu's Dead End: It Can't Be Diluted, So It Must Be Drunk Neat

Baijiu's tragedy is that it cannot even be rehydrated.

Apart from the light-aroma style, baijiu mixed with anything tastes of koji and plastic solvent — undrinkable, and no top brand is exempt. At an event in Beijing's Guomao district years ago, Guojiao was a sponsor and served martinis made with its 1573. They hired an excellent bartender; the glassware and the olives were professional. It did not matter. It smelled wrong and tasted worse.

Why? Baijiu's selling point is precisely its cause of death. Beyond alcohol and water, baijiu carries heavy loads of esters and acids, and premium brands brag about exactly those numbers. But chemistry has a counterintuitive rule: if a solute makes up 1% of a solution, getting it to 2% means removing half the solvent. A fruit that doubles its sugar content has long since shriveled into a raisin. Western spirits are a light seaweed-and-egg soup; baijiu is a tonic broth with seven pounds of ribs and a turtle shell thrown in.

Cut the proof in half and you must add an equal volume of water — yet the esters and acids are still there, and the koji flavor still punches through. Nobody can drink 20% sauce-aroma baijiu; it tastes like diluted vomit. So baijiu is left with exactly one way to be drunk: neat. And neat is, of all methods, the one that destroys the body most thoroughly.

Whisky Gets No Exemption Either

Do not mistake this for bashing China and praising foreigners. Neat baijiu is 24-karat; neat whisky is a solid 18. Whisky simply gets diluted with ice more often, so the self-harm is less flagrant.

Whisky's problem is that it is expensive and still not the real thing. A blended whisky is no different from a supermarket baijiu — blenders mixing vats, carefully respecting the brand's internal price ladder so the cheap bottle never upstages the dear one. The single casks they worship? The law allows topping them up with water to fill the bottles. Cask strength? Different casks can be blended to hit the advertised proof — blending again. The trade calls it “strengthening”: take a cheap, high-proof, flavorless liquid and pour it into an expensive, low-proof, flavorful one to top up the alcohol and stretch the age statement. Fully legal.

Blending is the unavoidable path for almost all whisky, which makes it an industrial product, no different from motor oil. And in the end, you will probably add ice anyway — someone pre-diluted it for you.

The Health Bill Was Always Due

That alcohol causes cancer is settled science, written in plain conclusions. China just prefers not to look. Drinking spirits neat devastates the lining of the mouth, the esophagus, and the stomach: on top of alcohol's own carcinogenic dose, it stacks a concentration spike. A 2% solution full of ice and watermelon and a 52% solution are not in the same league when it comes to burning tissue.

Then there is the liver. Ethanol metabolizes into acetaldehyde, which is fiercely toxic to the liver — and East Asians very commonly carry a genetic defect that keeps them from clearing acetaldehyde properly. It pools in the liver, kills liver cells, and the dead cells trigger inflammation that suppresses the surrounding tissue. It is like paying off one predatory loan with another: you die faster. Ten late nights are nothing next to one all-nighter — everyone understands that arithmetic.

China's stomach cancer incidence and mortality are both far above America's, with worse outcomes. Someone in the comments always pipes up that Americans drink even more. Fine — suppose they do. Then the conclusion only gets uglier: with less heavy drinking than America, China produces far more stomach cancer. In a country already loaded with salt, nitrites, and Helicobacter pylori, drinking 50-proof-plus spirits neat is just stacking debuffs on yourself and asking why the boss fight is hard.

As if whoever drinks himself to death wins a medal. That logic itself needs rehab.

Abolish baijiu distillation at the source and allow only beer, wine, and anything at or under 20%, and stomach cancer rates would fall off a cliff. No study needed — it follows by logic, the way a faster connection makes a game play better. Anyone can follow it.

Real Chinese Drinking Culture Is Not the Still

People who argue with me about health always retreat to “drinking culture.” Unfortunately, the thing they are defending is precisely the part with no culture in it.

China's ancestors took wine seriously, down to the characters they coined for it. Low-alcohol, slightly sweet brews were called lao; served with the rice grains still in, laozao; the ferment itself, nie. The clear, slightly stronger stuff — ten percent at most — earned the name jiu. Its microbe was qu, its craft was yun, and each additional feeding of qu raised the count: up to nine feedings, jiuyun. Qu was cultivated across generations, kept by recipe, tended by specialists, treated almost as a conduit to the gods. Every wine word in the old books refers to that grain wine tradition.

When Li Bai wrote of “clear wine in a golden cup, worth ten thousand cash,” he meant the finest grain wine of the age: a dozen percent at most, carried from the ice cellar in a silver pot, dosed with herbs, smelling of grain and cool air, pouring amber. That is wine worth He Zhizhang pawning his golden turtle for, worth calling its drinker a banished immortal. Li Bai was not drinking postpartum rice wine — but he was certainly not drinking shaoguo either.

So the true heir of orthodox Chinese wine is, ironically, industrial lager brewed from rice and barley: grain ingredients, the yun fermentation method, merely sealed to keep the carbon dioxide in and bittered with hops, which is why you call it beer. As for traditional huangjiu, I will not promote it, for a simple reason: it does not taste good. The dry style does not taste good either.

The Young Have Already Voted With Their Feet

The right way to drink has been obvious all along: dilute it, ice it, bring the proof down.

I have a recipe that never fails. One-third of a big blue bottle of Red Star Erguotou, half a bottle of coconut milk drink, one bottle of vitamin C soda, half a can of Red Bull, diced watermelon, and three big bags of ice, all in one large basin. The coconut and watermelon bring sweetness, the vitamin soda brings acid, the Red Bull buries the alcohol taste. Stir and taste as you go, like tossing a northeastern cold salad, until it is refreshing and you cannot taste the alcohol at all. It costs almost nothing and it is genuinely delicious. Everyone gets a paper cup and ladles it out — exactly like the outlaws in Water Margin quenching their thirst with rice wine. I have watched a woman who swore she was allergic to alcohol and never drank drain cup after cup of it, face flushed red.

Red wine works the same way. However expensive the bottle, add ice and Yakult without hesitation — the bigger and more tannic the wine, the better it tastes cut. At a nightclub, my first move is to order an ice bucket, then ice everything all night; people call me the Ice Bucket Prince. Even fake Chivas cut with green tea and drowned in ice does less damage than neat baijiu.

And that elegant movie shot — the Westerner who comes home and pours a finger of spirits from a glass bottle? Live abroad and you learn: without heating, the night is truly cold. Skip that drink and the bed itself is ice; you cannot sleep. One year I lived on New Zealand's North Island during the World Cup, with matches at 2 to 4 a.m. Leaving a friend's place at four, I was so cold the key would not go into the ignition, and I shook the whole drive home. One match, Germany against Brazil, was already 4–0 at the twenty-fifth minute. Frozen stiff, I decided the rest was garbage time, went home, mixed whisky with a little cola, and slept like a stone — then woke to learn it had finished 7–1, a bloodbath, and I have regretted it ever since. In that climate, spirits are a heating tool, not a cultural totem.

One last, radical suggestion. If you are a man in the high-carb north, over 150 jin, with a calendar full of baijiu banquets, get yourself a tirzepatide pen and start with 5mg before we discuss drinking at all. You will very likely discover you were never addicted to alcohol. The baijiu lover actually wants the fatty dishes that come with it. The beer lover actually wants the carbs. Block the signal, and you will not be able to finish half a can of light lager.

That is when you will truly understand: all that “drinking culture” was nonsense.

Chinese people have not lost the ability to drink. I will say it once more: they have simply become civilized, and learned to value their own lives. There is a wonderful world out there waiting to be enjoyed. Drinking yourself to death in your fifties is a waste — a bad trade by any measure.
excerpt_en: Baijiu output has fallen 74% from its 2016 peak, and everyone asks why China can't drink anymore. The real answer: distilled spirits were a logistics hack dressed up as culture, and a healthier generation is walking away.
title_en: China Hasn't Forgotten How to Drink. It Has Finally Learned How to Live.
